channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] A cyberattack has kept a Chilean solar-and-battery plant off the grid for almost three months, and no one has said which control systems were hit
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Chile’s National Electric Coordinator still lists the 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant in the Tarapacá region, and its 98 MW / 312 MWh battery system (still in commissioning), at zero availability in its 14 November report, recorded as a forced outage caused by a cyberattack. T13 dates the attack to 26 August; the coordinator activated its disconnection protocol on 27 August, after the company reported the incident, to protect the power system. Its cybersecurity director called the incident exceptional but says the investigation is confidential. The same records show a forced disconnection of a transformer at the Santa Rita substation on 27 August with a cyberattack cause, and losses of supervisory control at the Olivos and Espinos thermal plants that the report says were later ruled out. On 11 November a member of Congress asked whether notification duties under Chile’s cybersecurity law were met, and which systems (SCADA, remote control, protection, inverters, battery management) were compromised and whether third-party remote access was involved; no answer had been published by 16 November. The owner, entry route and attacker are undisclosed. For renewable and storage operators the lesson is that a plant disconnected for safety can stay dark for months if it cannot show its control systems are clean (editorial assessment). - ESS News / pv magazine (17 Nov 2026, citing Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional records); T13 (16 Nov 2026, in Spanish); pv magazine Latin America (16 Nov 2026, congressional requests, in Spanish) - Ongoing — still offline per 14 Nov 2026 coordinator report; congressional requests 11 Nov 2026; reported 16–17 Nov 2026; attack 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
item.category: Incident — PHP2Shell plus Gaia root flaw CVE-2026-123039 used to backdoor Check Point gateways and wipe a VMware ESXi host (wave 1 from 30 Oct, Israel; wave 2 from 2 Nov, multiple countries); CVE-2026-123039 added to CISA KEV 13 Nov 2026
item.description: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment). - Check Point Research (12 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1154 (12 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov); CISA KEV alert (13 Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (Nov 2026) - Wave 1 from 30 Oct 2026; wave 2 from 2 Nov 2026; research published 12 Nov 2026; KEV addition 13 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Ransomware halts smart-meter production and shipments at Japan’s Osaki Electric
item.category: Incident — Ransomware at Japanese smart-meter maker Osaki Electric (confirmed 17 Nov 2026); production and shipments suspended at its Saitama centre and group plants (reported 18 Nov 2026); no group named
item.description: Osaki Electric, a Japanese smart-meter maker, said ransomware encrypted data on its servers on 17 November. It cut its systems off from outside networks and suspended production and shipments at its Saitama R&D and manufacturing centre and at group companies Iwate Osaki Electric and Osaki Platech; NHK reported the production-management system was among those knocked out. On 20 November the company said the intruder most likely got in on 15 November through a VPN device, by password guessing against an account without multi-factor authentication; some virtual servers were encrypted and technical information believed to be its own was posted online. No group has claimed it, and nothing suggests field meters or electricity supply are affected. For utilities, the risk is supply-chain: delayed meter rollouts, and how suppliers protect the systems that build and sign their devices (editorial assessment). - Osaki Electric announcements, via TipRanks (17 Nov 2026; updated 18 and 20 Nov 2026, entry route and data leak); NHK (18 Nov 2026, in Japanese); Kyodo, via Yahoo! Japan News and Tokyo Shimbun (18 Nov 2026, in Japanese) - Intrusion estimated 15 Nov 2026; attack confirmed 17 Nov 2026; entry route disclosed 20 Nov 2026; no production restart reported

item.title: [High] Illinois investigates an apparent cyberattack attempt on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River
item.category: Incident — Attempted cyberattack on the state-run Algonquin Dam, Fox River, Illinois (16 Nov 2026; disclosed by IDNR 20 Nov 2026); dam kept secure and operating; CISA and state agencies investigating; no attribution
item.description: The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said on 20 November that it detected an apparent attempted cyberattack on the Algonquin Dam, about 45 miles northwest of Chicago, on 16 November. Staff blocked the unauthorised access at once, and the dam stayed secure and fully operational. IDNR has not said which system was targeted or whether gate controls were reachable. Illinois State Police, state agencies and CISA are investigating; no link to other attacks and no group has been named. For dam owners, hydro operators included,, it is a prompt to check who can reach gate and spillway controls remotely (editorial assessment). - CBS Chicago (20 Nov 2026); ABC7 Chicago (20–21 Nov 2026); BNO News (21 Nov 2026); all citing the Illinois Department of Natural Resources - Attempt 16 Nov 2026; disclosed 20 Nov 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [Medium] Equinor says the cyberattack on its IT systems has been stopped after three days, as a second Norwegian energy firm reports an attempted attack
item.category: Incident — Cyberattack on certain IT systems at Norway’s Equinor, disclosed 17 Nov 2026 and declared stopped on 20 Nov 2026; production unaffected throughout; Skagerak Energi reported an attempted attack on 18 Nov 2026; no attribution
item.description: Equinor, Norway’s state-controlled energy company and the EU’s largest pipeline-gas supplier, said on 20 November that the cyberattack on certain IT systems it disclosed on 17 November has been stopped. Production ran normally throughout, and it has found no sign that data was stolen or altered. Equinor says the attack was not a self-spreading virus and did not appear aimed specifically at it; police and Norway’s National Security Authority, which raised the national cyber risk level to “high” on 27 October, are involved. A day after Equinor’s first report, Skagerak Energi, a power and renewables utility in eastern Norway, reported an attempted attack with operations unaffected. Neither has disclosed the entry route or attacker, and nothing points to OT. Two incidents at Norwegian energy firms in one week are reason to check IT-to-OT boundaries now (editorial assessment). - Rigzone (20 Nov 2026, attack stopped; Skagerak Energi attempted attack); Riviera Maritime Media (20 Nov 2026, timeline of Equinor updates and NSM risk level); Equinor statements (17–20 Nov 2026); Reuters (19 Nov 2026, attack still ongoing); The Record (18 Nov 2026) - Disclosed 17 Nov 2026; declared stopped 20 Nov 2026; Skagerak attempt reported 18–19 Nov 2026

item.title: [Low] AVEVA says intruders accessed its corporate SharePoint; it reports no impact on its software or production environments
item.category: Incident — Unauthorized access to an OT software vendor’s internal document repository; vendor says its software is not affected
item.description: AVEVA had posted security bulletin AVEVA-2026-007 by 23 October (the entry carries no date of its own), saying it is investigating unauthorized access to its corporate SharePoint, an internal document repository. AVEVA says the issue does not affect its software and platforms, and that its software and production environments are separate from SharePoint and were not affected. It has activated its incident-response plan, brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement, and says it will notify third parties if the investigation finds material impact on them. It recommends no customer action and has not said what documents, if any, were viewed or taken, or who was responsible. AVEVA software is widely used across power, oil and gas, water and manufacturing, so customers should ask whether their own project documents were kept in the affected repository (editorial assessment). - AVEVA security bulletin AVEVA-2026-007 on its cyber security updates page (primary) - Posted by 23 Oct 2026; no incident date disclosed

item.title: [Low] Engie says attackers took French customers’ contact and supply-point details from a partner marketing tool; its own systems were not breached
item.category: Incident — Customer-data breach at a partner marketing tool; no operational impact
item.description: In customer notices reported on 27 October, Engie said it had found unusual data access in a tool that its business partners use to prospect for customers and market energy offers in France. It cut off the access, says the incident is limited to customers in France, and says its internal IT systems were not compromised. The notification letters list names, postal and email addresses, phone numbers, the PDL or PCE supply-point identifier, customer ID and contract number; Engie says no banking data was involved. It has not said how many customers were affected or when the access began, no group has claimed the breach, and no operational impact has been reported. This is a third-party, IT-side breach, but real supply-point and contract numbers make utility-themed phishing far more convincing (editorial assessment). - Engie statement and customer notification letters, reported by BleepingComputer (27 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (28 Oct 2026) - Disclosed 27 Oct 2026; further coverage 28 Oct 2026; detection date not disclosed

item.title: [High] Lumen: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay chains have carried zero-day attacks on network-management platforms since 2023, and energy is among the targeted sectors
item.category: Threat Intelligence — China state actor’s relay network used to exploit management-platform zero-days; energy among named sectors
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on 28 October describing Silent Train, a framework Volt Typhoon has used since about November 2023 to reach management and control-plane systems. Each operation runs through a short-lived chain of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment that is torn down after use, which makes the source hard to trace. Lumen ties four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one to the group: N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812) and Versa Director, with Quest KACE assessed as a likely zero-day; the CVEs it names are in KEV. These are earlier flaws than the Cisco SD-WAN Manager and VeloCloud flaws carded on this page, and Lumen does not tie those to Volt Typhoon. Black Lotus Labs says it has sent hundreds of victim notifications over about three years; named sectors include telecoms, government, defence, managed service providers and critical infrastructure in water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services. No utility victim is named and no OT intrusion is described. Lumen advises keeping administrative interfaces off the internet, patching management and control-plane systems first and extending log retention, and points to CISA’s AA24-038A and AA26-113A. For utilities, the SD-WAN orchestrators and remote-management tools that link control centres to field sites are the kind of platform this actor goes after (editorial assessment). - Lumen Black Lotus Labs, “Silent Train” research, 28 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by CyberScoop and Zero Day, 28 Oct 2026; CISA KEV - Published 28 Oct 2026; activity observed since November 2023

item.title: [High] France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
item.category: Threat intelligence — Iran-linked sabotage of internet-reachable controllers (France: IRGC attribution 9 Nov 2026; EU sanctions decision expected 14 Dec 2026); relevance to power operators is editorial assessment
item.description: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against the people behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers, freezing their assets and barring travel, a day after EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed new Iran sanctions are being prepared. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites, putting donor blood and therapies at risk. US and Israeli officials have told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. For OT defenders the lesson is plain: any internet-reachable controller is now a proven target. - Arab News, from AFP (17 Nov 2026, Barrot: EU decision expected 14 Dec); APA (18 Nov 2026, Barrot on France 5: sanctions within a month); dpa, via Yahoo News (16 Nov 2026, Kallas: EU sanctions in preparation); Asharq Al-Awsat and The New Arab (16 Nov 2026, French sanctions push); Health-ISAC (16 Nov 2026, cold-chain bulletin); Wall Street Journal (13 Nov 2026), via Newsmax wire on Yahoo News and Voice of Emirates; RFI via AOL (11 Nov 2026, Paris prosecutor’s warrant request); The Record (9 Nov 2026, French attribution and at least 15 fires); Insurance Journal, from Reuters (13 Nov 2026, BSI warning); Bytes Europe (13 Nov 2026, CCB warning); Midnight Blue (Nov 2026, AK-SM 800A research); GBHackers (13 Nov 2026); NPR (9 Nov 2026, Iranian denial); Iran International (14 Nov 2026, IRGC response); Arab News, from AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement) - Barrot: EU sanctions within a month 17–18 Nov 2026; EU confirms sanctions in preparation, French sanctions push and Health-ISAC bulletin 16 Nov 2026; WSJ report 13 Nov 2026; BSI and CCB warnings 13 Nov 2026; warrant request 11 Nov 2026; French attribution 9 Nov 2026; IRGC rejects French findings 14 Nov 2026; October attack 11–12 Oct 2026; investigations ongoing

item.title: [Medium] DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
item.category: Government threat assessment — DHS Secretary’s written testimony to the House Homeland Security Committee (18 Nov 2026); DNI and DHS tell the same hearing recent US outages were not cyberattacks
item.description: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For OT owners, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers. - Jerusalem Post (18 Nov 2026, Mullin written testimony); Report.az (18 Nov 2026); Bloomberg (18 Nov 2026); Federal News Network (18 Nov 2026, outages not a coordinated attack); Washington Examiner (18 Nov 2026, hearing); AttackIQ “Weighing Cyber Power”, via Water Online (17 Nov 2026) - Testimony and hearing 18 Nov 2026; AttackIQ research 17 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
item.category: Research — Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis for Q3 2026 (published 16 Nov 2026), covering July–September; Check Point October 2026 statistics (12 Nov 2026) for comparison
item.description: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October. - Dragos (16 Nov 2026); Australian Cyber Security Magazine (17 Nov 2026); Check Point Research October 2026 statistics, via iTWire (12 Nov 2026) - Published 16 Nov 2026; data covers July–September 2026

item.title: [Critical] Siemens adds WTV676 and WTV776 metering gateways to its PHP2Shell advisory, while parts of Spectrum Power still have no fix
item.category: Advisory — Exploited PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CISA KEV) in Siemens grid-control, metering and energy products; SSA-166980 V1.5, 18 Nov 2026; ABB and Schneider Electric OT products also listed
item.description: Siemens revised SSA-166980 to V1.4 on 16 November to add its WTV676 and WTV776 metering gateways to the products affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both in CISA KEV), and to V1.5 on 18 November with a fix for WTV676-HB6035: firmware FW6.9.22-3.4. WTV776-HB6035 has no fix. Grid-control parts also remain unfixed: Spectrum Power 4 with Nagios or Zabbix, Web Office Portal V3.0 to V3.2 and HISViews V1.0, plus AMIS TS and two blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 models; Energy Engage V2.0SP9 will get no fix. Spectrum Power 3 and 7 take Red Hat’s PHP patches, Spectrum Power TG needs PHP 8.5.12 and Energy Engage V3.1SP1 PHP 8.1.34 release 6. ABB lists its Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways and Schneider a Foxboro DCS server. No Siemens, ABB or Schneider product is reported exploited, but the same flaws have been used to root PAN-OS firewalls and Check Point gateways (see Incidents & Attacks), so an exposed web front end next to grid control is a real foothold (editorial assessment). - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-166980 V1.5 (18 Nov 2026; V1.4 16 Nov, V1.2 29 Oct) (primary); CISA KEV (26 Oct 2026); ABB and Schneider Electric advisories (29–30 Oct 2026) - First published 26 Oct 2026; metering gateways added 16 Nov 2026; WTV676 fix 18 Nov 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers try to plant bots on Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 edge gateways through a CVSS 10 Node-RED flaw
item.category: Advisory — Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Node-RED missing authentication, CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS 10.0, SSA-834709); exploitation attempts seen by VulnCheck from 30 Oct 2026
item.description: VulnCheck reported that from 30 October attackers were trying to exploit CVE-2026-58115 against its honeypots. The flaw, rated CVSS 10.0, is missing authentication in the Node-RED HTTP interface on SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed: an unauthenticated attacker can create flows that run code with maximum privileges. The first attempts deployed a flow that downloaded and ran a Linux bot; later ones used a two-stage downloader, and some added an HTTP endpoint wired to an exec node, a backdoor that survives a reboot even if a memory-resident implant is lost. Siemens published SSA-834709 in August; the fix is Node-RED 4.3.4.1 or later, or removing Node-RED. Only honeypots were hit, and no compromise of a real device has been reported. IoT2050 boxes are used as data-collection gateways at substations and generation sites, so look for ones you did not know about (editorial assessment). - The Hacker News (3 Nov 2026, citing VulnCheck); Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709 (Aug 2026) - Exploitation attempts from 30 Oct 2026; reported 3 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — VMware vCenter authentication bypass CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) exploited as a zero-day for more than two months by a suspected China-linked group, per Mandiant; Broadcom fix released 19 Nov 2026; no public fix for vCenter 7.0
item.description: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment). - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Broadcom, Google Threat Intelligence/Mandiant and Mandiant CTO Charles Carmakal); CISA KEV alert (20 Nov 2026); The Hacker News (20–21 Nov 2026) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; patched 19 Nov 2026; exploited from at least early Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
item.category: Active exploitation — Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8), clustered Expressway Core/Edge; exploited after a public PoC (reported by F6); added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; fixed in X15.5.20
item.description: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to plant-side systems (editorial assessment). - Security Affairs (21 Nov 2026, CISA KEV additions of 20 Nov); SecurityWeek (Nov 2026, citing F6); Security Affairs (20 Nov 2026, F6 findings) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 18–20 Nov 2026; patched 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Arista says a VeloCloud Orchestrator flaw that lets any logged-in user take operator control is being exploited; CISA’s deadline has passed
item.category: Incident — Exploited SD-WAN orchestrator flaw, CISA KEV
item.description: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 in Security Advisory 0199 on 22 October: an SQL injection in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) that lets any authenticated user, down to the Enterprise Read Only role, escalate to operator-level rights by impersonating a built-in superuser account. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4, says it found the issue itself and that it is known to be actively exploited, and lists two source IP addresses to block. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, now passed. Releases 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12 fix it; hosted orchestrators, including Dedicated ones, were also affected and Arista has already patched them. Arista notes that the orchestrator’s web interface is exposed by default. No actor, victim or sector has been named. The orchestrator pushes configuration to the SD-WAN edges that link offices, plants and remote sites, so operator access is a position from which paths toward field sites could be changed (editorial assessment). - Arista Security Advisory 0199, 22 Oct 2026; CISA KEV listing, 23 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Security Affairs and The Hacker News - Disclosed 22 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
item.category: Advisory — OpenJDK “Java4Shell” memory-corruption flaw CVE-2026-114938 (disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026); exploitation attempts seen 18–19 Nov 2026; Siemens SSA-272816 lists three Industrial Edge Management products
item.description: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched. - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Calif, GreyNoise, WatchTowr, Cloudflare, Previdian, Siemens SSA-272816, Cisco and Atlassian); The Record (18 Nov 2026, CISA alert) - Disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026; exploitation attempts 18–19 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
item.category: Active exploitation — N-able N-central: 4EverAble2Shell exploited to plant miners (13 Nov 2026); N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and removes the Legacy API (16–17 Nov 2026); separate breach of N-able’s hosted Mail Assure/SpamExperts cloud disclosed 20 Nov 2026
item.description: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (20 Nov 2026, Mail Assure/SpamExperts breach); The Hacker News (17 Nov 2026, Hotfix 3, citing N-able release notes of 16 Nov); The Hacker News (13 Nov 2026, citing Huntback and Previdian); The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026, new chains); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Tenable (10 Nov 2026) - Mail Assure breach disclosed 20 Nov 2026; Hotfix 3 released 16 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 13 Nov 2026; Able2Shell disclosed 9 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Mitsubishi Electric fixes critical authentication-bypass flaws in ICONICS GENESIS64 and GENESIS; MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz get no fix
item.category: Advisory — SCADA/HMI and historian suite, authentication bypass and permission flaws, no known exploitation; three products get no fix
item.description: Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006, published 15 October, covers ICONICS GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX, plus MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. CVE-2026-16436 (CVSS v4.0 9.2) is an authentication bypass: a fixed, shared challenge-response unlocks any user account, although a remote attacker must first obtain that response. CVE-2026-16438 (v4.0 9.4) stems from default DCOM permissions granted to the administrator account, and CVE-2026-16437 (v4.0 7.1) lets an administrator read or write the challenge-response file. The bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (v4.0 9.3) affects GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite 10.97 to 10.97.2 but needs a local administrator to import a crafted file. Fixes are in ICONICS Suite and IoTWorX 10.98, GENESIS 11.04 and, for libwebp, 10.97.3. There will be no fix for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz; Mitsubishi tells users to migrate or apply mitigations. No exploitation of ICONICS products is reported, and none of the ICONICS-specific flaws is in KEV; the bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 has been in KEV since 13 September 2023 because of browser exploitation. CISA republished the advisory on 27 October as ICSA-26-300-02, listing CVSS v3.1 scores of 9.1 for CVE-2026-16438, 8.1 for CVE-2026-16436, 6.4 for CVE-2026-16437 and 8.2 for CVE-2023-4863. ICONICS HMI and historian software is used across energy and utility operations, so these servers often sit close to control networks (editorial assessment). - Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory 2026-006, 15 Oct 2026, and CISA republication ICSA-26-300-02, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV record for CVE-2023-4863 via CIRCL - Published 15 Oct 2026; CISA republication 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Hitachi Energy TRO600 wireless routers let an unauthenticated attacker read configuration and password files; firmware 9.2.2.1 fixes it
item.category: Advisory — Industrial wireless router firmware, unauthenticated file read, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA republished Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000224 on 29 October as ICSA-26-302-02; Hitachi Energy and the CVE records date it 27 October. It covers firmware for the TRO600 series, which Hitachi Energy describes as high-throughput, low-latency industrial wireless communications devices used by utilities, oil and gas companies and mining operators. CVE-2026-106087 (CVSS v3.1 7.5 in CISA’s advisory; v4.0 8.7 from Hitachi Energy) is missing authentication: an unauthenticated attacker can read or download arbitrary files on the device, including configuration files and password data, in firmware 9.1.1.0 and earlier. CVE-2026-10756 (v3.1 7.5; v4.0 7.7) lets an authenticated attacker use port forwarding to get past network access restrictions and reach services meant to be reachable only from the device itself, in 9.2.1.6 and earlier. Firmware 9.1.2.0 fixes the first flaw and 9.2.2.1 fixes both; Hitachi Energy recommends 9.2.2.1. The advisory’s summary mentions remote code execution, but neither flaw description does. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known exploitation. Configuration and password data taken from a field-network router could give an attacker the credentials and network layout to reach substations and other remote sites (editorial assessment). - Hitachi Energy PSIRT advisory 8DBD000224, 27 Oct 2026, and CISA republication ICSA-26-302-02, 29 Oct 2026 (primary); CSAF and CVE records via CIRCL; product description from Hitachi Energy - Vendor advisory 27 Oct 2026; CISA republication 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa: its remote-access client can be fooled into trusting a fake server, and the end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway gets no fix
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and end-of-life cellular gateway flaws; no fix for the gateway; no known exploitation
item.description: Moxa published MPSA-269510 on 27 October. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6) affects the client for Moxa Remote Connect Suite (MRC), its OpenVPN-based remote-access service: versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0 accept configuration supplied by the server without proper certificate validation, so an attacker on the network path could impersonate the server. Version 4.2.2 fixes it and is available through Moxa support. The same advisory covers the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (7.7) is a set of static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (7.5) lets a privileged remote attacker inject commands through SMS management when that feature is enabled. Moxa considers the gateway end-of-life and will not fix it; its mitigations are to reset the device so it generates new keys and to keep SMS management disabled, as it is by default. No exploitation has been reported. Cellular gateways like this often link remote substations, reclosers and DER sites, and vendor remote-access clients are a common route to field devices (editorial assessment). - Moxa security advisory MPSA-269510, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE records via CIRCL; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Hitachi Energy CoreTec4 and CoreTec5: an authenticated command injection and a kernel root flaw with public exploit code; CoreTec4 owners must migrate
item.category: Advisory — Transformer-monitoring platform, authenticated command injection and kernel root escalation; no fix for CoreTec4
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-302-03, first released on 27 October and republished on 29 October from Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000258, covers CoreTec4 and CoreTec5 at 3.4.0 and earlier. Hitachi Energy says CoreTec technology powers its TXpert Hub monitoring system, part of its line for digitalizing transformers. CVE-2026-13162 (CVSS v3.1 7.5 in CISA’s advisory; v4.0 7.7 from Hitachi Energy) is an OS command injection in the configuration daemon’s time-zone handler: an authenticated user with certain roles can run arbitrary system commands and take full control. CoreTec5 is also affected by the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, which lets a local low-privileged user become root; CISA’s assessment notes public proof-of-concept code, and the sources disagree on its score. CoreTec5 5.0.0 fixes both. CoreTec4 has no fixed version, and the remedy is migrating to CoreTec5 5.0.0. The CVE record for CVE-2026-13162 lists CoreTec5 up to 5.0.0 as affected, which conflicts with the advisory, so confirm the fixed version with Hitachi Energy. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known exploitation; neither flaw is in KEV, and the kernel flaw is a different one from CVE-2026-46300, which is. A compromised monitoring device on a substation network is a foothold beside protection and control equipment (editorial assessment). - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-302-03, 27 Oct 2026, republished 29 Oct (Hitachi Energy PSIRT 8DBD000258) (primary); CVE records via CIRCL; product description from Hitachi Energy - Released 27 Oct 2026; CISA republication 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] DOE rules on barring grid equipment tied to covered foreign entities are due 24 December, and they could reach existing contracts
item.category: Regulation — Executive Order 14421 (26 Aug 2026) on foreign-produced bulk-power equipment; DOE implementing rules due 24 Dec 2026
item.description: Executive Order 14421, signed on 26 August, lets the Energy Secretary prohibit buying, importing, transferring or installing foreign-produced bulk-power equipment tied to a “covered foreign entity”, at its core Chinese entities. A 27 October POWER Magazine analysis by Vinson & Elkins lawyers notes the prohibition applies notwithstanding existing contracts, and that DOE’s implementing rules, due by 24 December, will decide which equipment and manufacturers are covered and whether licences are available. DOE’s FAQ (updated 6 October) lists transformers, breakers, protective relays, generators, grid-connected inverters, battery storage and industrial control systems, and says associated software, firmware, remote access and services may count; foreign origin alone does not trigger a ban. Nothing is barred yet. For OT teams the practical step is an accurate inventory of installed and ordered control, protection and inverter equipment, and of who can reach it remotely (editorial assessment). - POWER Magazine (27 Oct 2026, Vinson & Elkins analysis); DOE Bulk-Power System EO and RFI FAQ (updated 6 Oct 2026) - Published 27 Oct 2026; DOE rules due 24 Dec 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s 2030 strategy names OT asset visibility and intrusion detection as priorities and starts a review of its core services within 60 days
item.category: Policy — CISA four-year strategy; OT security named as a priority
item.description: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October, a four-year strategic plan introduced by Acting Director Nick Andersen. It commits the agency to help critical-infrastructure operators improve OT security, including asset visibility and intrusion detection, and to focus resources where they will have the greatest effect, informed by infrastructure assessments that include a UK-style national risk register. CISA will begin reviewing its core services and capabilities within 60 days, complete an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days, and report on progress after a year. The plan creates no new obligations for operators, and the coverage reviewed does not single out the electric sector. For utilities, the practical question is which CISA services they rely on today and how the service review changes them (editorial assessment). - CISA strategy “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail”, 26 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Cybersecurity Dive and CyberScoop, 26 Oct 2026 - Released 26 Oct 2026; service review to begin within 60 days
